extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of architecture, art historians, and educated readers interested in Venetian architecture and art theory
extracted.subtask_description: Critical and prescriptive guidance on Venetian (Byzantine and Gothic) architecture, decorative arts, and material-specific artistic practice, with moral and historical interpretation. The text sets aesthetic standards for how materials and forms ought to be used and judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate aims for given materials
rubrics_metrics.description: "All art, working with given materials, must propose to itself the objects which, with those materials, are most perfectly attainable; and becomes illegitimate and debased if it propose to itself any other objects, better attainable with other materials."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artist should set goals that the medium can achieve naturally; attempting effects better achieved in other media is illegitimate. Examples: intricate, ramified forms suit painting or metalwork, not sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor and exalt the peculiar qualities of materials
rubrics_metrics.description: "The workman...should even so far honor the materials with which he is working as to set himself to bring out their beauty, and to recommend and exalt, as far as he can, their peculiar qualities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the material's virtues manifest: in marble exhibit transparency and solidity; in iron, strength and tenacity; in gold, ductility. The material will 'be grateful' and the work becomes nobler for eulogizing its substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture must avoid expressing extreme slenderness or intricate fineness
rubrics_metrics.description: Great slenderness, lightness, or intricacy of structure (e.g., detached folds of drapery, wreaths of hair, birds' nests) is easily expressible in metalwork or painting, but only with great difficulty and imperfectly in sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculpture that aims chiefly to render such characters is 'debased.' If such suggestions are required, they should be given only to an extent compatible with perfect ease of execution in stone; generally only the general form and as much fibrous structure as can be easily represented should be attempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass-work principle: vessels should proclaim ductility; windows should proclaim transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass's two great qualities are its ductility when heated and its transparency when cold; in vessels we ought to exhibit ductility, and in windows, transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All work in glass is bad which does not loudly proclaim one or other quality. Very neat, finished, or perfect forms in glass are barbarous because they conceal ductility; for windows, the transparency and brilliant colors should be emphasized rather than pictorial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of cut glass and overly neat glass
rubrics_metrics.description: "Consequently, all cut glass is barbarous: for the cutting conceals its ductility, and confuses it with crystal. Also, all very neat, finished, and perfect form in glass is barbarous..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cutting or over-finishing glass objects; such treatment denies the material's essential character and represents a barbarism in technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painted windows must not be treated as oil pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to turn painted windows into pretty pictures is one of the most gross and ridiculous barbarisms... Glass, considered as a material for a picture, is exactly as bad as oil paint is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Windows reverse natural pictorial conditions (lights transparent, shadows opaque) and their color is ungovernable and violent when produced by actual light; therefore windows should avoid pictorial oil-like effects and not try to emulate easel-painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: True perfection of a painted window
rubrics_metrics.description: "The true perfection of a painted window is to be serene, intense, brilliant, like flaming jewellery; full of easily legible and quaint subjects, and exquisitely subtle, yet simple, in its harmonies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design stained glass to be jewel-like, vivid, and readable at a distance, using strong pure colors and simple harmonious composition rather than pictorial subtlety; medieval (12th–13th century French) examples are the ideal model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of workmanship for glass vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: "No workman ought ever to spend more than an hour in the making of any glass vessel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glass vessels are best when spontaneity and easy execution show the material's ductility; prolonged labor to attain fineness is inappropriate and wasteful of the medium's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material suitability determines acceptable detail and labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the physical properties of a medium, some effects are impossible or require intolerable labor; attempting these is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose forms and levels of detail that can be achieved 'with perfect ease' in the given material; don't force sculpture to emulate painting's intricacies or glass to be painted like oil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural expression should reflect social/spiritual conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as the cathedral of Torcello: built by exiles in flight and distress, its exterior 'is absolutely devoid of decoration' except certain carved entrances; internally the mosaics and arrangement express 'deep sorrow and the sacred courage' of its builders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form and ornament should be honest expressions of the builders' circumstances and purpose (e.g., humility, refuge), not artificial displays designed to attract or provoke; architecture must suit its moral and historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject romanticized or anachronistic readings of historic sites; prefer frank inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The Venice of modern fiction is 'a thing of yesterday... a mere efflorescence of decay... a stage dream'; romantic feelings may gild but 'never save the remains' and must be 'torn away' to see buildings in their own strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying historic architecture, abandon sentimental or dramatic fictions and perform careful, candid inquiry into the true nature, construction, and condition of the remains to restore an accurate understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windows and glass as spiritual/pedagogic instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass in church architecture expresses transparency as typical of the entrance of the Holy Spirit into the heart of man; its purity and brilliancy render it spiritually powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stained glass in ecclesiastical settings to convey spiritual symbolism via color and light rather than pictorial narrative; the material's qualities should serve theological/architectural meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for historical material-technical constraints in conservation/restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Venetian palaces have been modernized or altered (shafts shifted, capitals reused, arcades covered), producing anomalies in proportion; such changes fit modern uses but can destroy original effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In restoration, be mindful of original materials, proportions, and techniques; avoid insensitive modern interventions that disrupt ancient ornamentation and structural relationships—where change is necessary, acknowledge its impact on aesthetic and historical integrity.
